parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=3x^2+5x$.

Use the definition $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ to find the derivative of $f(x)$.

solutions.latex:
Expanding $f(x+h)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)&=3(x+h)^2+5(x+h)\\ &=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h \end{aligned}$$
so
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)-f(x)&=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h-(3x^2+5x)\\ &=6xh+3h^2+5h \end{aligned}$$
Using the definition:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{6xh+3h^2+5h}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\,(6x+3h+5) \end{aligned}$$
Apply the limit by letting $h=0$:
$$\therefore \dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x+5$$
criteria: Finds correct expression for $f(x+h)-f(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Rewrite so the limit takes the standard form $\displaystyle\lim_{\theta\to 0}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{5x}&=\dfrac{4}{5}\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 4x}{4x}\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\times 1\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave the answer 4/5 only; the standard-limit step added.

solutions.latex:
Using the definition of the derivative from first principles:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{5(x+h)^2-3(x+h)-(5x^2-3x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{5x^2+10xh+5h^2-3x-3h-5x^2+3x}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{10xh+5h^2-3h}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{h(10x+5h-3)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}(10x+5h-3) \\ &= 10x-3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly expands and simplifies, or equivalent merit
